title: STRIDE and the Birth of Formal Threat Modeling (1999)
explainer: In 1999, Microsoft engineers Loren Kohnfelder and Praerit Garg circulated an internal paper, "The Threats to Our Products," that organized attacker goals into six categories - Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege - giving threat modeling its first repeatable structure. STRIDE became the backbone of Microsoft's Security Development Lifecycle and is still the most widely taught way to walk a data-flow diagram and ask what can go wrong. Knowing it began as an internal memo rather than an academic theory underscores that threat modeling is a practical engineering habit, not a specialist's black art.

title: Saltzer and Schroeder's 1975 Design Principles for Secure Systems
explainer: Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder's paper "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems" distilled decades of operating-system experience into principles such as least privilege, fail-safe defaults, and complete mediation - the same checklist a secure-SDLC design review still applies today. The paper predates STRIDE by over twenty years, showing that most threat-modeling vocabulary accumulated gradually from hard-won lessons about how systems actually fail, rather than springing from one framework. Reading its plain-language list of eight principles clarifies why "secure by design" reviews ask the questions they ask.
